Nearly 90% y/y growth for the world's biggest car exporter is a bit crazy.

A stat I just dug up. From 1970 to 1980 Japan's auto exports increased from 1m cars to 4.5m cars, so +3.5m over ten years. China's car exports are poised to jump 3.5m in 2026 alone!

Hard to overstate the extent to which the global customs trade surplus is concentrated in a single region of the global economy.

East Asia's surplus in the last few months,annualized, is ~1.7 trillion.*

* would be even higher if China's gold imports were netted out https://t.co/a6p649l4mY

Bloomberg: China's robust car exports, up 88% year-on-year in July, contrast with the overall slump in domestic sales, which dropped 21%."
https://t.co/RFS9UrqOuw

Implication of all this, of course, is that the big fall in the bilateral deficit that the Trump Administration trumpets as one of the successes of tariffs isn't real -- as the Chinese goods just enter after taking a one stop flight through other jurisdictions

The comments section attacks @tylercowen for this post (https://t.co/c5beV1DyNE) because it shows nominal burrito prices have gone up 50% and the claim he misses the point plotting real burrito prices. Perhaps he should’ve said “burritos, which are getting all the attention, have gone up no faster than the general level of inflation.” But his overarching point is still valid as (Grok answer below) nominal wages (median not billionaire) have gone up slightly more. Burrito prices have stayed the same vs. CPI and gotten more affordable to the median earner as real incomes have gone up. Not the story both ass ends of the horseshoe want you to hear.
@cullenroche True in theory. But in practice is Gen Z day trading stocks and options against Citadel/Jane-St etc basically just as bad as betting on sports against the house?

A) If you own a passive fund you aren’t trading against them.

B) If you don’t you really still aren’t trading against them except perhaps at the super-short term (oh, don’t be super short-term). They mainly take the other side of your trades as market makers (and do so more cheaply than in generations past). That doesn’t mean you should day trade of course.

Not that this is what you guys are discussing but concentration is some degree of problem for a quant (or anyone) running long-only against and index. The problem is the negative alpha stocks can only be not owned and that can be a very small bet. Of course, self-serving plug alert, long-short investing (or even relaxing the no shorting constraint) makes this a non-issue (unless you think, really a totally separate thing, that a concentrated market tells you something about the future).
